title: Addition & Subtraction
blurb: Multi-digit addition and subtraction with regrouping, mental strategies, fact families with missing numbers, and multi-step word problems.

lessons.title: Adding with Regrouping
lessons.concreteComparison: Two herder families combine their flocks for the winter: $4\,586$ sheep and $2\,747$ sheep. Nobody counts the merged flock from scratch — you ADD, place by place, and whenever a place overflows past nine you trade ten of it for one of the next place up. That trade is the carry, and it is the only new move in all of column addition.
lessons.objective: Add multi-digit numbers with the column method, carrying (regrouping) through any number of places, and add three or more numbers by grouping them cleverly.
concept: **Line up the places.** Column addition works because ones add with ones, tens with tens, hundreds with hundreds — the place-value ladder from Topic 1 doing bookkeeping.

**Carry = trade ten for one.** When a column's sum passes $9$ — say $6 + 7 = 13$ — you cannot write two digits in one place. Trade: ten ones become one ten. Write the $3$, carry the $1$ into the tens column.
**Order is yours to choose.** Addition doesn't care about order or grouping, so with three numbers, pair the friendly ones first: $618 + 254 + 382$ goes fastest as $(618 + 382) + 254 = 1\,000 + 254$.
lessons.keyIdea: Add place by place from the ones; when a column passes nine, trade ten of it for one of the next place — that's the carry, and it's the whole algorithm.

facts.title: The carry
facts.explanation: Ten ones trade for one ten — the sum keeps one digit per place.

facts.title: Group the friendly pair
facts.explanation: Addition lets you reorder and regroup — hunt for sums that make round numbers.

workedExamples.note: Watch the carry travel through three columns.
workedExamples.solution: Ones: $6 + 7 = 13$ — write $3$, carry $1$. Tens: $8 + 4 + 1 = 13$ — write $3$, carry $1$. Hundreds: $5 + 7 + 1 = 13$ — write $3$, carry $1$. Thousands: $4 + 2 + 1 = 7$. Sum: $7\,333$.

workedExamples.statement: A tent costs $12\,485$ tögrög and a stove $9\,635$. What do they cost together?
workedExamples.note: Different lengths — align by place, not by first digit.
workedExamples.solution: Line up the ones: $12\,485 + 9\,635$. Ones: $5 + 5 = 10$ — write $0$, carry $1$. Tens: $8 + 3 + 1 = 12$. Hundreds: $4 + 6 + 1 = 11$. Thousands: $2 + 9 + 1 = 12$. Ten-thousands: $1 + 1 = 2$. Total: $22\,120$ tögrög.

commonMistakes.text: Writing the whole two-digit column sum in one place — 6 + 7 = 13, so writing "13".
commonMistakes.correction: One digit per place. Write the 3, TRADE the ten: carry 1 into the next column.

commonMistakes.text: Lining numbers up by their first digits instead of their last.
commonMistakes.correction: Align the ONES (the right edge). 12,485 + 9,635 lines the 5 under the 5 — the 9 sits under the 2, not under the 1.

tryIt.solution: Pair the friendly two first: $618 + 382 = 1\,000$, then $1\,000 + 254 = 1\,254$.

steps.title: The carry is a trade
beats: Column addition adds place by place, starting from the ones — the place-value ladder doing bookkeeping.
When a column passes $9$, you cannot write two digits in one place. TRADE ten of it for one of the next place: $6 + 7 = 13$ → write $3$, carry $1$.
The carry is not a rule to memorise — it is ten ones becoming one ten, the Topic 1 trade in action.

steps.title: Carries in action
steps.intro: Ones first; trade every overflow upward.

steps: Tens: $8 + 4 + 1 = 13$ — write $3$, carry $1$. Hundreds: $5 + 7 + 1 = 13$ — write $3$, carry $1$.
Align the ONES, not the first digits.

steps.title: Column sums
steps.intro: Ones first — and let the carries travel.

problems.explanation: Three carries in a row: $5\,222$. (Dropping the tens carry gives $5\,212$ — the classic slip.)
Align by the ones: $25\,706 + 4\,518 = 30\,224$ — the thousands column carries into the ten-thousands.

steps.title: Where does the 1 go?
steps.prompt: In the ones column you get $8 + 5 = 13$. What do you write, and what do you carry?
steps.explanation: Thirteen ones trade into one ten and three ones: the $3$ stays in the ones place, the $1$ joins the tens column.

steps.title: The abacus carries the same way
steps.body: On a Mongolian abacus (самбар тоолуур), when a rod fills past nine you clear it and push one bead on the next rod — a physical carry. The written algorithm is the abacus move in pencil form; both are the ten-for-one trade.

steps.title: Three numbers? Choose your order
beats: Addition doesn't care about order or grouping — so with several numbers, YOU choose the friendliest path.
$618 + 254 + 382$: spot the pair that makes a round number — $618 + 382 = 1\,000$ — then $1\,000 + 254 = 1\,254$.
Hunting for pairs that make tens, hundreds or thousands turns long sums into short ones.

steps.title: Friendly pairs first
steps.intro: Reorder to build round numbers, then finish.

steps.title: Pick the pair
steps.intro: Find the round-number pair before adding anything.

problems.prompt: The fastest first move for $246 + 588 + 754$ is:
problems.explanation: $246 + 754 = 1\,000$, then $1\,588$. The other orders work but fight the carries.

steps.title: Does order matter?
steps.prompt: Which is TRUE about $a + b + c$?
options: any order gives the same sum
you must add left to right
the biggest number must go first
steps.explanation: Addition is commutative and associative — every order and grouping gives the same total, so pick the friendliest: e.g. $2 + 9 + 8 = (2 + 8) + 9 = 19$.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Add place by place, starting from the ones.
A column past nine trades ten for one — write the digit, carry the 1.
Align numbers by their ONES, never their first digits.
With several numbers, pair the ones that make round numbers first.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Mixed column sums — say the carry out loud each time it happens; the dropped carry is this lesson's only real enemy.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Carries and clever grouping together.

problems.explanation: The carry ripples through every column: four nines roll over to $10\,000$.

problems.prompt: A school library has $6\,485$ books and buys $2\,738$ more. Now it has:
problems.explanation: $6\,485 + 2\,738 = 9\,223$ — carries in the ones, tens and hundreds.

steps.title: You've finished "Adding with Regrouping"
steps.body: Every carry you wrote was a ten-for-one trade up the place-value ladder. Next lesson runs the same trade BACKWARDS: subtraction, where a ten breaks back into ten ones.

lessons.title: Subtracting with Regrouping
lessons.concreteComparison: A concert hall printed $5\,003$ tickets and sold $1\,647$. How many remain? Column subtraction hits a wall at once: you cannot take $7$ from $3$. The fix is the carry run backwards — BREAK one of the next place into ten of this one. Borrowing is just un-trading.
lessons.objective: Subtract multi-digit numbers with the column method, borrowing (regrouping) through any place — including across zeros — and check every subtraction by adding back.
concept: **Borrow = break one into ten.** When a column's top digit is too small, break one unit of the next place into ten of this place: in $52 - 38$, break a ten so the ones read $12 - 8$.

**Across zeros, the break travels.** In $5\,003 - 1\,647$ the ones need a ten, but the tens and hundreds are $0$ — so the break walks left: a thousand breaks into ten hundreds, one of those into ten tens, one of those into ten ones.
**Addition is the receipt.** Every subtraction can be checked: answer $+$ what-you-took-away must rebuild what-you-started-with. $5\,003 - 1\,647 = 3\,356$ because $3\,356 + 1\,647 = 5\,003$.
lessons.keyIdea: Borrowing is the carry run backwards — break one of the next place into ten of this one — and every answer can be checked by adding back what was subtracted.

facts.title: The borrow
facts.explanation: One ten breaks into ten ones; the tens column drops by one.

facts.title: The add-back check
facts.latex: a - b = c \iff c + b = a
facts.explanation: The answer plus the subtracted amount must rebuild the original.

workedExamples.solution: Ones: $4 < 8$, break a ten: $14 - 8 = 6$. Tens: now $4$, and $4 < 7$, break a hundred: $14 - 7 = 7$. Hundreds: now $1$, and $1 < 4$, break a thousand: $11 - 4 = 7$. Thousands: $7 - 3 = 4$. Difference: $4\,776$. Check: $4\,776 + 3\,478 = 8\,254$.

workedExamples.statement: The hall printed $5\,003$ tickets and sold $1\,647$. How many remain?
workedExamples.solution: The ones need a ten, but tens and hundreds are $0$: break the thousand — $5\,003$ regroups as $4$ thousands, $9$ hundreds, $9$ tens, $13$ ones. Now subtract: $13 - 7 = 6$, $9 - 4 = 5$, $9 - 6 = 3$, $4 - 1 = 3$: $3\,356$ tickets. Check: $3\,356 + 1\,647 = 5\,003$.

commonMistakes.text: Flipping the digits instead of borrowing — reading 2 − 8 as "8 − 2 = 6".
commonMistakes.correction: The columns are not symmetric: 52 − 38 is 14, not 26. When the top digit is smaller, BORROW; never swap.

commonMistakes.text: Forgetting that a borrowed-from digit shrinks by one.
commonMistakes.correction: Breaking a ten leaves one fewer ten. Mark the break (cross out, write the new digit) — unmarked borrows are the top source of wrong answers.

tryIt.statement: Subtract $7\,132 - 4\,815$, then check by adding back.

tryIt.solution: Break across the zeros: $6\,000$ becomes $5$ thousands, $9$ hundreds, $9$ tens, $10$ ones. $6\,000 - 2\,384 = 3\,616$; check $3\,616 + 2\,384 = 6\,000$.

steps.title: Borrowing is the carry, backwards
beats: When a column's top digit is too small — $2 - 8$ won't go — BREAK one of the next place into ten of this one.
$52 - 38$: break a ten. The $5$ tens become $4$, the $2$ ones become $12$: now $12 - 8 = 4$ and $4 - 3 = 1$. Answer $14$.
It is exactly the addition carry run in reverse: there you traded ten-for-one going up; here one breaks into ten coming down.

steps.title: Breaks in action
steps.intro: Mark every break — the lender shrinks by one.

steps: Ones: break a ten — $14 - 8 = 6$. Tens: break a hundred — $14 - 7 = 7$.
Ones: tens are $0$, so the break travels — a hundred breaks into ten tens, one ten into ten ones: $13 - 8 = 5$.

steps.title: Column differences
steps.intro: Borrow where needed; mark the lender.

problems.explanation: Borrows in the ones and hundreds: $2\,317$. Check: $2\,317 + 4\,815 = 7\,132$.
$2 - 8$ needs a borrow: $12 - 8 = 4$, then $4 - 3 = 1$. ($26$ comes from illegally flipping to $8 - 2$.)
Break a ten for the ones ($16 - 9 = 7$); the rest follows: $7\,247$.

steps.title: Spot the illegal flip
steps.prompt: A student computes $63 - 47 = 24$, reading the ones as "$7 - 3$". The true answer is:
steps.explanation: Columns don't flip: $3 - 7$ needs a borrow — $13 - 7 = 6$, then $5 - 4 = 1$: $16$. The flip error ($24$) fails the add-back check: $24 + 47 = 71 \ne 63$.

steps.title: Cashiers subtract by adding
steps.body: Old-school market change-making runs subtraction as addition: for a $6\,350$ tögrög purchase paid with $10\,000$, the seller counts UP — "$6\,350$, $6\,400$ ($50$), $7\,000$ ($600$), $10\,000$ ($3\,000$)" — handing you $3\,650$. Adding up IS subtraction; next lesson makes it a strategy.

steps.title: Zeros, and the receipt
beats: Subtracting from a number full of zeros — $5\,003 - 1\,647$ — sends the break TRAVELLING: the thousand breaks into ten hundreds, one hundred into ten tens, one ten into ten ones.
After the travelling break, $5\,003$ reads as $4$ thousands, $9$ hundreds, $9$ tens, $13$ ones — and the subtraction runs smoothly.
Always collect the receipt: answer $+$ subtracted $=$ original. $3\,356 + 1\,647 = 5\,003$ — if the receipt fails, the subtraction was wrong.

steps.title: Across the zeros
steps.intro: Let the break travel, then subtract column by column.

steps.title: Zero-crossing subtraction
steps.intro: Regroup once, then every column has enough.

problems.explanation: The break travels through four zeros: $5\,725$. Receipt: $5\,725 + 4\,275 = 10\,000$.
The receipt: answer plus subtracted rebuilds the original — $446 + 356 = 802$. ✓

steps.title: The travelling break
steps.prompt: To subtract the ones in $700 - 258$, the ten you need comes from:
options: a hundred breaking into tens, then one ten into ones
steps.explanation: The tens are $0$, so the break travels: one hundred → ten tens, one of those → ten ones. $700$ reads as $6$ | $9$ | $10$, and $700 - 258 = 442$.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Borrowing breaks one of the next place into ten of this one — the carry in reverse.
Never flip a column: when the top digit is smaller, borrow.
Across zeros, the break travels leftward until it finds a nonzero digit.
Collect the receipt: answer + subtracted = original, every time.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Every problem below has a receipt — run it. If answer + subtracted misses the original, find the unmarked borrow.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Borrows, zeros, receipts.

problems.explanation: Ones: $0 - 5$ needs a ten from the $5$ tens — $10 - 5 = 5$, tens now $4 - 2 = 2$. Hundreds: $0 - 3$ breaks a thousand — $10 - 3 = 7$, thousands $7 - 4 = 3$: $3\,725$. Receipt: $3\,725 + 4\,325 = 8\,050$ ✓.

problems.prompt: A granary held $9\,000$ kg of flour and shipped $3\,485$ kg. It still holds:

options: not possible with whole-number answers here — the second number is bigger
problems.explanation: Subtraction of whole numbers needs the first number to be at least the second: $5\,556 > 5\,555$. (Negative numbers arrive in later grades.)

problems.prompt: Which answer FAILS its receipt: someone claims $7\,403 - 2\,168 = 5\,335$?
problems.explanation: $5\,335 + 2\,168 = 7\,503 \ne 7\,403$: an unmarked borrow. The true difference is $5\,235$.

steps.title: You've finished "Subtracting with Regrouping"
steps.body: Carry up, break down — the two directions of one trade. And the receipt habit (answer + subtracted = original) will guard every subtraction you ever do. Next: doing all this in your head, faster than the written method.

lessons.title: Mental Addition & Subtraction
lessons.concreteComparison: The market price is $499$ tögrög and you buy that item plus one for $276$. No paper needed: charge yourself $500$, add $276$ to get $776$, hand back the borrowed $1$ — total $775$. Round numbers are easy numbers, and the whole art of mental arithmetic is trading your problem for a round-number one, then repaying the trade.
lessons.objective: Add and subtract mentally using compensation (round, then repay), making tens and hundreds, and counting up — and choose the strategy that fits the numbers.
concept: **Compensation:** move a number to the nearest round one, compute, then repay. $499 + 276$: do $500 + 276 = 776$, repay the borrowed $1$: $775$. Works for subtraction too — $1\,995 + 2\,468 = 2\,000 + 2\,468 - 5$.
**Make a ten (or hundred):** split one number so a piece completes the other. $47 + 38$: take $3$ from the $38$ to complete $47 \to 50$, then $50 + 35 = 85$.
**Count up for subtraction:** the cashier's move. $1\,000 - 674$: climb $674 \to 700$ ($26$), then $700 \to 1\,000$ ($300$) — total climbed $326$, and that IS the difference.
lessons.keyIdea: Trade your problem for a round-number problem, then repay the trade — compensation, making tens, and counting up are all this one idea.

facts.title: Compensation
facts.explanation: Round, compute, repay — the borrowed amount comes back at the end.

facts.title: Counting up
facts.explanation: The distance climbed IS the difference — subtraction as a journey.

workedExamples.solution: $499$ is one short of $500$. Compute $500 + 276 = 776$, then repay the borrowed $1$: $776 - 1 = 775$.

workedExamples.note: Climb to the next round numbers.

commonMistakes.text: Repaying the compensation in the wrong direction — 499 + 276 = 776 + 1.
commonMistakes.correction: You ADDED an extra 1 when you rounded 499 up, so you must SUBTRACT it back: 775. Ask: did rounding make my problem bigger or smaller?

commonMistakes.text: Using the written algorithm in your head for numbers built for a strategy.
commonMistakes.correction: Mental column-subtraction of 1,000 − 674 juggles three borrows. Counting up does it in two easy hops. Look at the NUMBERS before picking the method.

steps.title: Compensation — borrow a round number
beats: Round numbers are easy numbers. Compensation trades your problem for a round one, then repays: $499 + 276 \to 500 + 276 = 776$, repay $1$: $775$.
The repay direction follows the trade: rounded UP means you added too much — subtract it back. Rounded the subtracted number up? You took too much — add it back.

steps.title: Round, compute, repay
steps.intro: Say the repay out loud — direction is everything.

steps: Take $2\,000$ instead: $3\,000 - 2\,000 = 1\,000$ — but that took $2$ too many.

steps.title: Compensate
steps.intro: Round to the friendliest neighbour; repay at the end.

problems.explanation: Take $300$: $704 - 300 = 404$; you took $1$ too many — return it: $405$.

steps.title: Which way is the repay?
steps.prompt: You compute $825 - 498$ as $825 - 500 = 325$. To finish, you:
steps.explanation: Taking $500$ instead of $498$ removed $2$ extra, so give them back: $325 + 2 = 327$.

steps.title: The 99-price trick
steps.body: Shops price things at $1\,990$ or $9\,900$ partly because the leading digit reads small. Mental compensators are immune: you instantly see $1\,990$ as "$2\,000$ minus $10$" — and the till total stops being a surprise.

steps.title: Making tens, and counting up
beats: **Make a ten:** split one addend to complete the other. $47 + 38$: move $3$ across — $50 + 35 = 85$. Nothing was rounded, so nothing to repay.
**Count up** turns subtraction into a journey: $1\,000 - 674$ climbs $674 \to 700$ ($+26$) $\to 1\,000$ ($+300$): difference $326$. Two easy hops instead of three borrows.
Choose by the numbers: near a round number → compensate; digits that complete each other → make tens; subtracting from a round number → count up.

steps.title: Two more tools
steps.intro: Split to complete; climb to compare.

steps: Climb total: $326$ — that IS the difference.

steps.title: Pick your tool
steps.intro: Compensate, make tens, or count up — the numbers tell you.

steps.title: The cashier's move
steps.prompt: You pay for a $6\,350$ item with $10\,000$. Counting up, the change is:

steps.title: What you learned
points: Compensation: round, compute, repay — direction of the repay follows the trade.
Make a ten: split one number to complete the other; nothing to repay.
Count up: subtraction as a climb — the distance IS the difference.
Read the numbers first; they tell you which tool is fastest.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Do every one of these in your head — no columns. If you catch yourself borrowing mentally, look again for the round-number trade.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: All three tools, your choice each time.

problems.explanation: Count up: $1\,996 \to 2\,000$ ($4$), $\to 2\,003$ ($3$): $7$. No borrows needed at all.

steps.title: You've finished "Mental Addition & Subtraction"
steps.body: The written algorithm always works; the mental strategies win whenever the numbers are friendly — and prices, times and scores usually are. Next: the deep link between adding and subtracting, and the missing-number puzzles it unlocks.

lessons.title: Fact Families & Missing Numbers
lessons.concreteComparison: You saved some money, spent $456$ tögrög, and have $789$ left. How much did you start with? Nobody hands you the subtraction — you REBUILD it: what you have plus what you spent, $789 + 456 = 1\,245$. Addition and subtraction are one relationship read in two directions, and once you see that, every missing-number puzzle solves itself.
lessons.objective: Use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to write fact families, check computations, and solve missing-number equations.
concept: **One family, four facts.** The triple $456, 789, 1\,245$ makes four true statements: $456 + 789 = 1\,245$, $789 + 456 = 1\,245$, $1\,245 - 456 = 789$, $1\,245 - 789 = 456$. Same relationship, four readings.

**The whole and its parts.** In every family there is one WHOLE ($1\,245$) and two PARTS. Addition builds the whole from parts; subtraction finds a missing part. Ask first: is the unknown the whole, or a part?

**Missing numbers:** $\square - 456 = 789$ — the unknown is the whole (it was there before the spending), so ADD: $789 + 456 = 1\,245$. But $350 + \square = 1\,000$ — the unknown is a part, so SUBTRACT: $1\,000 - 350 = 650$.
lessons.keyIdea: Addition and subtraction are one whole-and-parts relationship read in two directions: the unknown whole comes from adding the parts, an unknown part from subtracting the other part from the whole.

facts.title: The fact family
facts.explanation: Four facts, one relationship — two additions, two subtractions.

facts.title: Whole or part?
facts.latex: \square - b = c \Rightarrow \square = c + b \qquad a + \square = c \Rightarrow \square = c - a
facts.explanation: Name what's missing first; the operation follows.

workedExamples.statement: Check the subtraction $7\,254 - 3\,867 = 3\,387$ using its fact family.
workedExamples.note: The family's addition rebuilds the whole.
workedExamples.solution: If the claim is right, then part $+$ part $=$ whole: $3\,387 + 3\,867 = 7\,254$. It does — the subtraction is correct.

workedExamples.note: Is the unknown the whole or a part?
workedExamples.solution: The box lost $456$ and still shows $789$ — the box is the WHOLE. Rebuild it: $\square = 789 + 456 = 1\,245$. Check: $1\,245 - 456 = 789$. ✓

commonMistakes.text: Always subtracting when a problem shows a minus sign — solving □ − 456 = 789 as 789 − 456.
commonMistakes.correction: Name the unknown first. In □ − 456 = 789 the box is the WHOLE, and wholes are rebuilt by ADDING: 789 + 456.

commonMistakes.text: Writing a fact family with the whole in a part's position, like 456 − 1,245 = 789.
commonMistakes.correction: The whole (the biggest number) leads every subtraction and ends every addition. 1,245 leads: 1,245 − 456 = 789.

tryIt.statement: Write the four facts of the family $350, 650, 1\,000$.

steps.title: One relationship, four facts
beats: Three numbers where two parts build a whole — $456$, $789$, $1\,245$ — make a FACT FAMILY: two additions and two subtractions, all saying the same thing.
This is why addition CHECKS subtraction (last lesson's receipt): they are the same relationship read in opposite directions.

steps.title: Families at work
steps.intro: The whole ends the additions and leads the subtractions.

steps: Parts $3\,387$ and $3\,867$ must rebuild the whole $7\,254$.

steps.title: Family membership
steps.intro: The whole is the biggest — it anchors all four facts.

problems.prompt: Which fact belongs to the family of $280$, $520$, $800$?
problems.explanation: The whole $800$ leads subtractions and ends additions: $800 - 520 = 280$. ✓

problems.prompt: Which triple is NOT a fact family?
problems.explanation: $120 + 340 = 460 \ne 480$ — the parts don't build that whole. (The other two close: $150 + 350 = 500$, $220 + 380 = 600$.)

steps.title: Read it backwards
steps.prompt: $5\,003 - 1\,647 = 3\,356$. Which fact is in the same family?
steps.explanation: Parts $1\,647$ and $3\,356$ rebuild the whole: $1\,647 + 3\,356 = 5\,003$ — the receipt from last lesson IS the fact family.

steps.title: Algebra is impatient fact families
steps.body: In a few grades you'll write x − 456 = 789 and "add 456 to both sides". That's exactly today's move — the unknown is the whole, rebuild it by adding — wearing algebra's clothes. You're doing algebra already; it just doesn't have letters yet.

steps.title: Whole or part? Then solve
beats: Every missing-number equation asks ONE question: is the box the WHOLE or a PART?
$\square - 456 = 789$: the box had $456$ removed and $789$ remains — the box is the whole. Rebuild: $789 + 456 = 1\,245$.
$350 + \square = 1\,000$: the box is a part of $1\,000$. Take the other part away: $1\,000 - 350 = 650$. Name the unknown; the operation follows.

steps.title: Solve for the box
steps.intro: Name whole-or-part BEFORE choosing the operation.

steps: The box is the whole (it lost a part and shows the rest).
The box is a part of the whole $5\,000$.

steps.title: Missing numbers
steps.intro: Whole → add the parts. Part → subtract the other part.

problems.explanation: The box is the whole: $640 + 275 = 915$. (Subtracting instead gives the trap answer $365$.)
The box is the part that was removed: $4\,000 - 1\,725 = 2\,275$; check $4\,000 - 2\,275 = 1\,725$ ✓.

steps.title: Name the unknown
steps.explanation: Something lost $830$ and still shows $1\,450$ — it must be the whole: $1\,450 + 830 = 2\,280$.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Three whole-and-parts numbers make four facts — two additions, two subtractions.
Addition checks subtraction because they are the same relationship, read backwards.
Missing number? Name it first: whole → add the parts; part → subtract the other part.
The whole is the biggest number — it ends additions and leads subtractions.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For every box below, say "whole" or "part" OUT LOUD before computing — the naming is the skill.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Families, receipts, and boxes.

steps.title: You've finished "Fact Families & Missing Numbers"
steps.body: Whole-and-parts thinking is the skeleton under every equation you will ever solve. Last stop in this topic: word problems that need TWO or three of these moves in a row.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Word Problems
lessons.concreteComparison: A shop opens with $12\,450$ tögrög in the till, takes in $3\,780$ in the morning and $4\,265$ in the afternoon, then pays a $8\,900$ delivery bill. Nobody solves that in one operation — you take it one EVENT at a time, writing the running total after each. Multi-step problems are just single-step problems standing in a queue.
lessons.objective: Solve word problems needing two or more additions and subtractions: track a changing total, compare amounts, and check the result against an estimate.
concept: **One event, one operation.** Read the story and list what happens in order: gained → add, lost → subtract. Compute a running total after each event; never try to hold two steps in one.
**Grouping is allowed.** Losing $3\,780$ then $4\,265$ is the same as losing $(3\,780 + 4\,265)$ at once — combine the like events first if it's friendlier: $12\,450 - 8\,045$.
**Estimate as the guardrail.** Round the numbers, run the same steps, and the exact answer must land near the rough one — a Topic 1 habit that catches dropped steps and misread signs.
lessons.keyIdea: Break the story into events, one operation each, running total after every step — and let a rounded version of the same plan check the answer.

facts.title: Events in order
facts.explanation: Losses can be taken one by one or bundled — same result.

facts.title: Comparison asks for a difference
facts.explanation: More/fewer/left-over questions are subtractions in disguise.

workedExamples.statement: A shop's till holds $12\,450$ tögrög. The morning brings in $3\,780$ of takings and the afternoon $4\,265$ more; then the shop pays a supplier $8\,900$ from the till. How much is in the till at closing?
workedExamples.note: List the events with their signs first.

workedExamples.statement: A library owns $8\,540$ books. It receives a donation of $1\,260$ and lends out $2\,375$. How many books are on its shelves?
workedExamples.note: Two events: a gain and a loss.

commonMistakes.text: Adding every number in the story because they're there.
commonMistakes.correction: Numbers don't tell you their sign — EVENTS do. "Lends out 2,375" is a loss. List the events with + or − before touching the arithmetic.

commonMistakes.text: Answering the wrong question — computing the afternoon takings when the problem asked for the till total.
commonMistakes.correction: Re-read the question sentence LAST, after solving: does your number answer exactly what was asked?

tryIt.statement: A train leaves with $845$ passengers. At the first stop $278$ get off and $164$ get on. How many ride on?
Two schools collected paper: one gathered $4\,320$ kg, the other $3\,485$ kg. How much more did the first school collect?
tryIt.solution: "How much more" is a difference: $4\,320 - 3\,485 = 835$ kg.

steps.title: One event, one operation
beats: A multi-step story is single steps in a queue. Read it and LIST the events in order: gained → $+$, lost → $-$.
Then compute a RUNNING TOTAL, one event at a time: till $12\,450$, $+3\,780 \to 16\,230$, $+4\,265 \to 20\,495$, $-8\,900 \to 11\,595$.
Never juggle two steps at once — the queue exists so each move is easy.

steps.title: Running totals
steps.intro: Sign the events first; then it's just arithmetic.

examples.prompt: Till $12\,450$; takings $3\,780$ and $4\,265$; a bill of $8\,900$ paid. Final till?
Library: $8\,540$ books, $+1\,260$ donated, $-2\,375$ lent. On the shelves?

steps.title: Queue the events
steps.intro: Sign each event, then run the total.

problems.prompt: A train carries $845$; $278$ get off, $164$ get on. Riding on:
problems.explanation: $845 - 278 = 567$, then $+164$: $731$. ($567$ answers only half the story.)

problems.prompt: A herder has $1\,240$ sheep, sells $385$, buys $150$. Now:
A water tank holds $9\,000$ L; $2\,450$ L is used, then $1\,780$ L more. Remaining:

steps.title: Same answer, two roads
steps.explanation: Two losses in a row equal one combined loss: $12\,450 - 8\,045 = 4\,405$ — same as subtracting them one at a time.

steps.title: Accountants call it a ledger
steps.body: A business's account book is exactly your running total: every gain and loss on its own line, the balance recomputed after each. Five-hundred-year-old Venetian bookkeeping and your word-problem method are the same technology.

steps.title: Comparisons, and the estimate guardrail
beats: "How many MORE", "how much LESS", "what's LEFT" — comparison words always ask for a DIFFERENCE: larger minus smaller.
Two schools collect $4\,320$ and $3\,485$ kg: "how much more" $= 4\,320 - 3\,485 = 835$ kg.
Guardrail every answer with an estimate: run the SAME event queue on rounded numbers. Exact and rough must land together — if not, hunt the dropped step.

steps.title: Compare and check
steps.intro: Differences for comparisons; estimates as guardrails.

examples.prompt: Schools collect $4\,320$ kg and $3\,485$ kg. How much more did the first gather?

steps: Exact was $11\,595$ — beside the estimate, so the plan held. ✓

steps.title: Comparisons
steps.intro: Larger minus smaller — then receipt it.

problems.prompt: A mountain is $3\,905$ m, another $2\,760$ m. The first is taller by:
Saturday's fair drew $6\,214$ visitors, Sunday's $5\,975$. Sunday drew fewer by:
An answer of $20\,495$ for the till problem (estimate $11\,000$) means:
options: a step was missed — the $8\,900$ bill was never subtracted
problems.explanation: $20\,495$ sits far from the $11\,000$ guardrail — and indeed $12\,450 + 3\,780 + 4\,265 = 20\,495$ is exactly the total BEFORE the bill. Subtracting the $8\,900$ gives the true $11\,595$.

steps.title: Which question was asked?
steps.prompt: "A farmer had $2\,400$ bales, sold $850$, then baled $600$ more. How many NOW?" The answer is:
steps.explanation: $2\,400 - 850 = 1\,550$, then $+600 = 2\,150$. ($1\,550$ answers the story only halfway through.)

steps.title: What you learned
points: List the story's events with signs; run the total one event at a time.
Like events can bundle: two losses = one combined loss.
Comparison words (more, fewer, left) ask for larger minus smaller.
Guardrail with an estimate run on the same plan — big gaps mean dropped steps.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Write the event list for each problem before computing — the list is where these are won and lost.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Full stories, start to finish.

Which estimate guards the wallet problem above?
problems.explanation: Same plan, rounded numbers: about $9\,000$ — the exact $7\,870$ lands near it. The other options run a different plan entirely.

practice.statement: Subtract $9\,213 - 5\,847$, then check by adding back.

practice.solution: The break travels across the zeros: $7\,000 - 3\,254 = 3\,746$; receipt $3\,746 + 3\,254 = 7\,000$ ✓.

practice.statement: A cinema sold $2\,485$ tickets on Friday, $3\,178$ on Saturday, and $1\,940$ on Sunday. How many more tickets did the weekend days (Saturday + Sunday) sell than Friday?

testYourself.solution: The break travels through the zeros: $3\,563$; receipt $3\,563 + 6\,437 = 10\,000$ ✓.

testYourself.statement: A claimed result says $8\,205 - 3\,647 = 4\,658$. Run the add-back check and give a verdict.
testYourself.solution: Receipt: $4\,658 + 3\,647 = 8\,305 \ne 8\,205$ — wrong. The true difference is $4\,558$.

testYourself.statement: A warehouse stores $18\,500$ boxes. It ships $6\,720$ and $4\,915$, then receives $2\,300$. How many boxes does it hold, and what rounded estimate guards the answer?
